data.title: Collection - Does mangrove restoration imply coastal protection? A prospective simulation study - Frontiers in Marine Science - Figshare
data.content:
# Does mangrove restoration imply coastal protection? Posted on 2022-09-23 - 06:04.

Mangrove restoration in the coastal zones is a concept proposed by environmental conservationists. Among the cited advantages of mangrove restoration are providing socio-economic services and coastal protection. Aware of these advantages, countries in Southeast Asia, such as the Philippines, have been implementing government- or civilian-backed restoration efforts. However, will current practices of restoration lead to the intended results? Also, are claims of coastal protection effects realistic? These two questions underscore the challenges posed by the long gap between the present intervention and future impact. Field evidence of protection may emerge from existing sites, the circumstances of which may not be easily portable onto other sites. This study examines the mangrove restoration practices in the Philippines and proposes the restoration index as a short-term prospective estimate of the future success of the restoration effort. This study also assesses the coastal protection potential of mangroves by examining the “bio-shielding” effect against storm surges driven by category-5 winds. Two coastal sites—Tacloban, Leyte, and Pan de Azucar, Iloilo—in the Philippines along the track of a category-5 storm, were considered. The restoration index was calculated based on the characteristics of Rhizophora mangroves commonly used in restoration programs. The coastal inundation model examined the extent of inland flooding due to storm surges by comparing an actual and hypothetical mangrove scenario for each site. A reasonable value of tree density obtained from the restoration simulations was estimated to determine if and to what degree, do mangroves in both sites offer coastal protection. For Tacloban, the actual mangroves are limited in scope, while the hypothetical scenario assumed a mangrove greenbelt fringing the city’s eastern periphery. For Pan de Azucar, the existing mangroves are dense at the southwestern tip of the island, whereas in the hypothetical scenario, these mangroves are absent. The results, reinforced with a household survey, indicated a positive economic value of mangrove restoration for coastal protection. The restoration index and coastal inundation simulations are prospective tools that will guide the Philippines and Southeast Asia, in general, in formulating impactful mangrove restoration programs.

data.title: Indonesia expands mangrove restoration to strengthen climate resilience and coastal protection | Indiplomacy
data.content:
Title: Indonesia expands mangrove restoration to strengthen climate resilience and coastal protection | Indiplomacy
# Indonesia expands mangrove restoration to strengthen climate resilience and coastal protection. *Source: Indonesian Ministry of Environment*. #### *Indonesia expands mangrove restoration through government, business and community collaboration*. Indonesia is accelerating mangrove restoration efforts by encouraging stronger collaboration between the government, businesses and local communities to strengthen climate resilience, protect coastal ecosystems, enhance food security and support sustainable economic growth. Indonesia’s Deputy Minister of Environment, Mr Diaz Hendropriyono, called on the private sector to participate in tree and mangrove planting programmes, stressing that restoring Indonesia’s shrinking mangrove forests is essential for improving air quality and mitigating the impacts of climate change. Beyond improving environmental resilience, mangrove restoration is also vital to safeguarding Indonesia’s fisheries and long-term food security. Speaking during the World Mangrove Day 2026 commemoration in Bali, Indonesia’s Minister of Marine Affairs and Fisheries, Mr Sakti Wahyu Trenggono, said rehabilitation efforts must restore ecosystem functions rather than focus solely on planting trees. Indonesia is home to around 23 percent of the world’s mangrove ecosystems, yet approximately 40 percent of its mangrove forests have been lost over the past three decades, with nearly one-fifth now classified as being in critical condition. To address these challenges, the Indonesian government is advancing mangrove restoration as part of its blue economy strategy, targeting the expansion of marine conservation areas to 97.5 million hectares by 2045. It is also revitalising 14,000 hectares of unproductive ponds along Java’s northern coast to integrate ecosystem restoration with sustainable aquaculture, job creation and national food security. APHI Chairman Mr Soewarso said rehabilitation success should be measured not only by the number of trees planted but also by ecosystem recovery, plant survival rates and improved livelihoods for coastal communities. Indonesia’s Deputy Minister of Forestry, Mr Rohmat Marzuki, said the ministry and its partners rehabilitated 91,678 hectares of mangroves by the end of 2025 and aim to restore more than 17,000 hectares in 2026. With continued collaboration among government agencies, businesses, development partners and coastal communities, Indonesia aims to accelerate mangrove restoration while strengthening climate resilience, protecting biodiversity, supporting sustainable fisheries and improving coastal livelihoods for future generations. #### LATEST. #### LATEST BOOKS.

data.title: Community-Based Mangrove Restoration for Enhanced Coastal Protection → Scenario
data.content:
Title: Community-Based Mangrove Restoration for Enhanced Coastal Protection → Scenario
Community-Based Mangrove Restoration (CBMR) stands as a beacon of hope in the increasingly urgent call for coastal resilience. At its core, CBMR recognizes that local communities, who are often the most intimately connected with and reliant upon mangrove ecosystems, are not merely beneficiaries of conservation efforts, but rather, they are the most effective agents of change. Looking ahead, the future of CBMR hinges on scaling up successful models, addressing the underlying drivers of mangrove degradation, and adapting to the accelerating impacts of climate change. If climate change impacts outpace the adaptive capacity of mangrove ecosystems and the effectiveness of CBMR efforts, the negative scenario of atrophy becomes increasingly likely. In this scenario, even well-intentioned and community-led restoration projects may be overwhelmed by the scale and speed of environmental change, leading to widespread mangrove dieback and increased coastal vulnerability. In a negative feedback loop, these social and economic disruptions can further undermine community capacity for CBMR and exacerbate the cycle of mangrove degradation and coastal vulnerability. Breaking this cycle requires proactive and integrated strategies that address both the ecological and socio-economic dimensions of CBMR, while also tackling the underlying drivers of mangrove loss and climate change. This empowered community model not only ensures the long-term sustainability of CBMR efforts, but also transforms communities into agents of broader social and environmental change. CBMR is therefore a nature-based solution that offers synergistic benefits for both climate mitigation and adaptation, making it a highly cost-effective and resilient approach to addressing climate change in coastal zones. This socio-economic transformation, driven by CBMR, creates more resilient and prosperous coastal communities, better equipped to face the challenges of climate change and sustainable development. The ascendancy scenario represents a future where CBMR is not just an environmental intervention, but a catalyst for positive social, economic, and ecological change, creating a virtuous cycle of sustainability and resilience in coastal regions worldwide. By embracing these principles and investing in CBMR as a strategic priority, we can unlock its transformative potential and usher in a future where coastal communities and mangrove ecosystems thrive together in a harmonious and resilient balance.

Title: Why are mangrove restoration projects important for coastal protection in Ecuador? | GoEco FAQ
# Why are mangrove restoration projects important for coastal protection in Ecuador? Mangrove restoration projects are crucial for coastal protection in Ecuador as they help stabilize shorelines, reduce erosion, and provide a natural barrier against storm surges and rising sea levels. These efforts support biodiversity and enhance the resilience of coastal ecosystems. * Mangroves play a vital role in stabilizing coastlines by trapping sediments and reducing erosion, which is essential for the protection of Ecuador’s coastal areas. * The dense root systems of mangroves provide a natural barrier against storm surges and rising sea levels, offering significant protection to coastal communities. * Restoration projects contribute to biodiversity by creating habitats for a wide range of marine and terrestrial species, thus enhancing the ecological health of the region. * Mangrove ecosystems are effective carbon sinks, sequestering carbon dioxide from the atmosphere, which is crucial in mitigating climate change impacts. * According to Stanford University’s research, mangrove restoration can significantly contribute to the global carbon cycle, highlighting its importance for environmental sustainability. Important to know: Participating in mangrove restoration projects in Ecuador may require physical labor and a commitment to environmental conservation efforts. For more about volunteering in Ecuador. data.title: Indonesia’s Mangrove Restoration: Practical Approaches for Coastal Protection and Climate Action FINCAPES Project
data.content:
Title: Indonesia’s Mangrove Restoration: Practical Approaches for Coastal Protection and Climate Action FINCAPES Project
# Indonesia’s Mangrove Restoration: Practical Approaches for Coastal Protection and Climate Action. Indonesia, home to nearly a quarter of the world's mangroves, faces significant challenges in protecting these vital ecosystems despite their crucial role in climate action, disaster risk reduction, economic resilience, and biodiversity. This brief, "Indonesia’s Mangrove Restoration: Practical Approaches for Coastal Protection and Climate Action," synthesizes key insights from the FINCAPES Project and its partners. It highlights persistent hurdles like governance issues (e.g., land tenure disputes, gender inequality), environmental factors (e.g., disrupted hydrology, poor site selection), and socio-economic barriers (e.g., weak incentives, limited local capacity). Through innovative approaches from projects like BRIN, Blue Forests, NASCLIM, and KTH Lestari, the brief showcases how site-specific restoration, hydrological rehabilitation, community-led education, and reframing mangroves as economic assets can drive success. Ultimately, effective restoration hinges on strengthening governance, implementing science-based approaches, and empowering local communities, particularly women. Discover the comprehensive strategies for scaling up these efforts and securing a sustainable future for Indonesia's invaluable coastal ecosystems.

Title: Mangrove Restoration for Coastal Defense → Scenario
# Mangrove Restoration for Coastal Defense. A prominent concentric ring highlights a high-fidelity environmental sensor, alongside an adaptive structural element crafted from multi-functional composites. This abstract composition features a glossy off-white component re-manufacturing unit and a dark blue autonomous resource conveyance system, both showcasing adaptive tooling interfaces. Mangrove forests, verdant sentinels of the coastlines, represent a critical nexus in the intricate web of global ecosystems and human societies. They offer a wealth of ecological services, with coastal defense standing as a paramount function in an era defined by escalating climate change impacts and rising sea levels. To truly grasp the significance of mangrove restoration for coastal defense, one must first undertake a comprehensive assessment of their current status, the threats they face, and the inherent capabilities they possess in safeguarding shorelines. Understanding this geographical context is essential as it immediately highlights the regions most vulnerable to mangrove degradation and, conversely, those that stand to gain most from successful restoration initiatives. However, assessing the current data also reveals a critical gap: while the ecological importance of mangroves is increasingly recognized, the translation of this awareness into effective, large-scale restoration is lagging. Furthermore, the drivers of mangrove degradation are often complex and deeply rooted in socio-economic systems. Therefore, a truly effective approach to mangrove restoration for coastal defense must be holistic, addressing not only the ecological aspects but also the social, economic, and political dimensions. The challenge is to move beyond recognizing the problem to implementing solutions that are both ecologically sound and socially equitable, ensuring the long-term protection of these vital coastal ecosystems and the communities that depend on them. The scientific community has produced a wealth of research solidifying the critical role of mangroves in coastal defense. Mangrove restoration projects are often implemented in coastal communities that are highly dependent on mangrove resources for their livelihoods. Local ecological knowledge is invaluable for site selection and restoration design, and community ownership is essential for ensuring the long-term protection of restored mangroves. It requires investing in capacity building, promoting local ecological knowledge, and addressing the underlying socio-economic drivers of mangrove degradation to ensure the long-term success of mangrove restoration for coastal defense.

data.title: Financing Mangrove Restoration for Coastal Defense → Scenario
data.content:
Title: Financing Mangrove Restoration for Coastal Defense → Scenario
The imperative to finance mangrove restoration for coastal defense is rooted in a confluence of ecological, economic, and social necessities. Payments for ecosystem services (PES) schemes offer another approach to incentivize mangrove conservation by directly compensating landowners or communities for the ecosystem services provided by mangroves, such as coastal protection, carbon sequestration, and fisheries enhancement. In summation, financing mangrove restoration for coastal defense demands a paradigm shift from reliance on traditional, often insufficient, funding sources towards innovative, diversified, and scalable financial mechanisms. Investing in mangrove restoration is not merely an environmental expenditure; it is a cost-effective investment in coastal protection, disaster risk reduction, and long-term economic stability. Avoiding this dystopian future requires a decisive shift towards prioritizing and adequately financing mangrove restoration as a critical investment in coastal resilience, ecological integrity, and social well-being. A future where financing for mangrove restoration is prioritized and scaled up presents a contrasting vision of coastal resilience, ecological recovery, and sustainable development. This ascendancy scenario, driven by innovative financial mechanisms and increased investment, unlocks the full potential of mangrove ecosystems to protect coastlines, sequester carbon, and support thriving coastal communities. The most tangible benefit of increased mangrove restoration financing is the strengthening of coastal defense. Mangrove restoration becomes not just an environmental imperative, but also an economic driver, contributing to sustainable coastal development and poverty reduction. In conclusion, the ascendancy scenario, driven by prioritized financing for mangrove restoration, offers a compelling vision of a sustainable and resilient coastal future. The potential benefits of mangrove ascendancy are immense, making it a worthwhile and urgent endeavor to invest in mangrove restoration as a cornerstone of coastal sustainability and climate resilience. The exploration of financing mangrove restoration for coastal defense reveals a critical juncture for coastal sustainability. How can insurance mechanisms be better utilized to recognize and reward the natural coastal protection provided by mangroves, and incentivize conservation and restoration? What are the long-term socio-economic impacts of mangrove restoration on coastal communities, and how can restoration projects be designed to maximize social benefits and minimize potential negative impacts? The future of mangrove ecosystems, and the coastal communities that depend on them, hinges on our collective commitment to prioritizing and adequately financing mangrove restoration.
